entries.title: Resort Connected to Jim Justice Ordered to Pay $52 Million for Defaulting on Pandemic Loan
entries.summary: The Greenbrier Resort’s finances have been mired in legal clashes.
entries.content:
A federal judge ordered The Greenbrier Resort, partially owned by the family of West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice, to repay $35 million in Main Street Lending Program funding, plus $17 million in interest, for defaulting on the loan.

The ruling on the unpaid pandemic loan is another chapter in the Justice family’s nearly 20-year ownership of the storied resort, which has also been mired in what the billionaire lawmaker recently described as “a highly complex legal dispute” over the resort’s future.

In this case, the loan was provided by First Guaranty Bank in Louisiana and chaired by businessman Marshall T. Reynolds, a Huntington, West Virginia, native. First Guaranty sued over the loan, which had been delinquent since December 2023, in a case that began in Louisiana before moving to the Southern District of West Virginia.

The judge, in an opinion Thursday, said there was no question Greenbrier defaulted and rejected the resort’s arguments why judgment should not be entered now.

The Greenbrier didn’t dispute that it missed payment, but contended the bank unfairly rejected a February 2025 proposal to push full repayment to the end of 2026, the opinion says.

The bank’s CEO testified that the Federal Reserve turned down the request by phone, although that was never put in writing, and nothing in the loan documents required the bank to agree to the proposal to extend the repayment date, the judge wrote.

Justice purchased the then-struggling historic resort in 2009, and handed day-to-day control to his daughter Jill when elected governor of West Virginia in 2016. Since the purchase, the resort has struggled with increasing debt. In late March 2026, the Rowling family, which owns Omni Hotels, paid $289 million to pay off the resort's first-lien debt.

The Justices sued, alleging Carter Bank and TRT Holdings, the parent company of Omni Hotels and Resorts, conspired to force them out. Omni’s subsidiary asked a federal court to appoint a receiver.

Earlier this year, the Justices announced an agreement with Kennedy Lewis Investment Management in an effort to bring financial stability to the resort, which ended the feud with Omni. The firm took 51% ownership of the resort company for a reported $500 million, leaving the Justice family with 49%.

The Greenbrier Resort, Kennedy Lewis Investment Management and the Justice family did not immediately return The Washington Sun’s inquiries.

A Government Accountability Office report in June found that 70% of the Main Street program’s loans had been fully repaid. The initiative was established in the CARES Act and was one of 13 emergency lending programs in response to COVID-19. The loans were supposed to be paid back by early January 2026.

The resort itself is over 100 years old, and sits on 11,000 acres of land in southern West Virginia. The resort also housed an underground emergency shelter for the United States Congress built during the Cold War before it was decommissioned after The Washington Post exposed it in 1992.
entries.author: Tyler Spence

entries.title: Sabres Beat Capitals, 6-3, In Fourth Straight Loss
entries.summary: Alex Ovechkin broke a tie with longtime teammate Nicklas Backstrom for Washington's career lead in assists with his 763rd.
entries.content:
By Noah Trister

Rasmus Dahlin and Beck Malenstyn scored 25 seconds apart in the first period to chase Logan Thompson, and the Buffalo Sabres sent Washington to its fourth straight loss, beating the Capitals 6-3 on Thursday night.

Jack Quinn scored twice — once into an empty net — and Zach Benson and Tage Thompson also scored for the Sabres. Buffalo converted on five of its 13 shots in the first two periods. Alex Tuch, Ryan Leonard and Boone Jenner scored Washington, which has fallen to .500 after entering the season with lofty expectations.

Alex Ovechkin broke a tie with longtime teammate Nicklas Backstrom for Washington's career lead in assists with his 763rd.

The Capitals have allowed at least five goals in four straight games and six of their last eight. On Wednesday it took them only two periods to do so. Thompson allowed three goals on five shots before being yanked in favor of Charlie Lindgren.

It was the second time in his last six starts Thompson was pulled early.

After Quinn opened the scoring, Dahlin entered the zone on a power play, and when Thompson overplayed him a bit to the near post, the Buffalo defenseman swooped behind the net and wrapped the puck into the vacated other side.

Malenstyn made it 3-0 and Thompson's night was done.

Tuch scored again against his former team. He had two goals against Buffalo, including the winner in overtime, in a game last month.

It was 4-1 after one Thursday, and Tage Thompson scored on the power play near the end of the second. Leonard scored to cap a dominant stretch on the power play for Washington in the third, then Jenner poked the puck in with 10:16 remaining after Buffalo goalie Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen seemed unaware it was loose.

Ovechkin received an assist on Jenner's goal, having passed to him in the neutral zone before Jenner dumped the puck toward the net, followed it and poked it in.

With neither team playing particularly well of late, Washington's Tom Wilson and Buffalo's Sam Carrick dropped the gloves right off the opening faceoff. Both were given fighting majors just one second into the game.

entries.title: Senators Pass Permitting Reform. Will It Survive the House?
entries.summary: An amendment process fell apart after objections from Democrats over a push to restrict data center development on public lands.
entries.content:
The Senate passed a permitting reform bill with bipartisan support Thursday evening, advancing legislation that would reshape the way major energy projects are built.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 passed 62-33.

Almost every Republican in the Senate voted in favor of the bill, which supporters say would cut red tape that holds back new power plants, factories and other infrastructure projects. Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Josh Hawley of Missouri were the two Republicans in opposition. Fifteen Democrats and Independents also supported it, saying the legislation would lead the country into a clean energy future and address climate-warming emissions. Both sides of the aisle argue the bill addresses affordability issues and would help reduce power bills.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), one of the bill’s core negotiators, told reporters she was “thrilled beyond words” after the bill passed and that the deal between four lawmakers from vastly different backgrounds was “monumentally legacy-setting for the country.” 

“I think we’ve got great momentum going into the House,” she said.

The legislation has been endorsed by trade groups from the American Petroleum Institute to the Solar Energy Industries Association and by several labor unions, including the AFL-CIO. It has splintered the environmental movement, though, with longtime climate hawks such as Al Gore and Bill McKibben speaking out against it, while it has attracted support from the advocacy groups Citizens’ Climate Lobby and Evergreen Action.

Several Senate Democrats dropped their support for the bill in recent days, expressing concerns over its effects on tribal sovereignty and changes to longstanding environmental laws like the Clean Water Act. They also grew concerned that it could be used to “lock in” fossil fuel development during the last two years of the Trump administration.

Senators spent Wednesday evening and Thursday negotiating an amendment process, which fell apart over demands from Oregon Democrats Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley. Merkley objected to the process itself, while Wyden was pushing for the inclusion of an amendment that would ban data centers on public lands.

Ultimately, Merkley blocked a vote on a bipartisan amendment from the bill’s sponsors that was meant to address concerns over tribal consultation and landowners’ compensation for transmission projects.

Late into the night on Thursday after the passage of the bill, Sen. Brian Schatz and Sen. Mike Lee, a core Republican negotiator of the bill, continued to push for the adoption of the bipartisan amendment as Merkley stood firm.

Lee accused Merkley of attempting to “sow fear, uncertainty and doubt, and put the bill in a position of vulnerability on the House side.”

Merkley said he blocked the amendment because of opposition to the permitting bill from tribes in the Northwest, and continued to push for other amendments that addressed data center concerns.

President Donald Trump has expressed his support for the bill. Its final hurdle is in the House, where both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries have indicated their support.

Efforts to amend the bill could derail its path forward, after months of negotiations between a bipartisan group of four senators culminated in a delicate deal.

Rep. Eric Burlison (R-Missouri) said he has concerns that the bill could lead to more cases of eminent domain being used in his district to build more transmission lines.

“My local concerns are, what it’s gonna do to farmers in Missouri to have a 300-foot tower being forced on their property and being given, basically, a pittance, so that California and Chicago can have more electricity,” he said.

Republicans are also worried about opening the door to more offshore wind projects and new clean energy subsidies, Burlison said. But ultimately, he said, there is “a lot of good” in the bill, calling House passage “achievable, but not a certainty.”

Democrats may continue advocating for further protections for the National Historic Preservation Act and environmental laws.

“I’m concerned about the Clean Water Act and the impact on tribal communities,” said Rep. Paul Tonko of New York, who sits on the Energy and Commerce Committee and said Democrats are split over whether to support the legislation in its current form.

Rep. Scott Peters (D-California), who supports the bill, said he would be open to changes, but it would be difficult for the House to make amendments in the short period of time left before the end of the session.

“I’m not sure how much, first of all, flexibility, but also institutional capacity we’re going to have to make amendments here,” he said. “We’re kind of up against the end of the clock.”

Peters added that the House has had input on the front end, saying he has met regularly with chief Senate negotiators.

Several Democrats have pushed to table permitting reform until next year when they’ll have majorities in the House and Senate. But Peters said waiting would be counterproductive.

“It lowers costs, it lowers emissions, we should pass it,” he said.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: ‘No Immediate Accountability’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 20, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

 In today’s newsletter: Mold problems, Rock Creek Tennis Center and a new column about D.C.’s people, places and parties.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 10/10. Another beautiful one, with sunshine and highs approaching 70 degrees. A happy high-five Friday for a top-tier day! Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

After last week’s deadly shooting in Logan Circle, an old foe has come back into focus: mold.

It was significant mold growth in shooter Matthew Lambert’s $1.1 million seventh-floor penthouse that spurred yearslong litigation and, tragically, his decision to take the life of building manager James Stuart and injure five other people.

Lambert’s violent response was an outlier. But the mold — and the complicated circumstances that many tenants and owners can face in D.C. when they find it — is not, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports.

Attorneys and housing advocates say D.C.’s mold laws and enforcement mechanisms frequently fall short for tenants — especially low-income ones. For years, D.C. charged one agency with inspecting housing conditions and another one with inspecting for mold.

“You had two sets of inspectors: two request portals, enforcement processes — everything was very separate,” said Carrie Tirrell, an attorney at the Children’s Law Center. That meant inspections and enforcement often happened slowly, if they happened at all, and actual consequences for landlords were infrequent.

The D.C. Council changed the law in 2020, putting all housing inspections — mold included — under the Department of Buildings. But the new law wasn’t funded for six years, and only started being implemented this October. Housing advocates are waiting to see whether the change makes life any better for tenants who might find mold.

In Lambert’s case, this change wouldn’t have made much of a difference. He owned his condo, after all. But given that he claimed the mold was caused by the building’s common elements, his attorney Joel Braithwaite thinks the city should consider requiring condo boards to address mold within 60 days of it being reported.

One tenant of a Northwest D.C. apartment told The Sun that the Logan Circle incident should spur more action by D.C. lawmakers.

“The process currently takes years and tens of thousands of dollars,” said Meighan Stone, who was displaced from her apartment late last year when significant mold was discovered. “That practically means there’s no immediate accountability.”





DEEP DIVE

In a win for disability advocates, the D.C. Council’s public works and operations committee unanimously decided Thursday to send a bill that would improve rideshare wheelchair accessibility to the full council for a vote.

Uber opposes the bill, but for its requirements around insurance, driver registration, surveillance pricing and data sharing, which it says will cause customer rates to go up. The company is launching an ad campaign today urging Washingtonians to oppose the bill. On Monday, Uber will send an email blast to its D.C. drivers, saying the company might end driver surges and incentives if the bill passes, meaning lower earnings and tips, according to a spokesperson.

“We can improve wheelchair-accessible vehicle service without the major price increases, driver restrictions, and unprecedented government surveillance that this bill entails,” LáVita Gardner, who leads Uber’s D.C. government affairs, told The Sun in a statement.

Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau, who chairs the committee and authored the bill, said that the measure just levels the playing field between rideshare and taxi companies, and that any data collected from rides will be anonymized.

“It's disappointing, when they tried to reach out to us during the AV discussion to be allies,” advocate Kelly Mack, who uses a powerchair, said of Uber’s opposition.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Game, set, lease: Local entrepreneur Mark Ein’s Rollingwood Sports struck a 60-year lease agreement with the Interior Department to operate Rock Creek Tennis Center, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

A decision is expected soon in the legal battle over whether the Kennedy Center can close its doors for two years of renovations. At a court hearing Thursday, plaintiffs urged the judge to reject the Trump administration’s request to lift a preliminary injunction blocking the closure, arguing that the center’s board continues to breach its fiduciary duties. The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports that, as an alternative, the plaintiffs suggested the judge could instead modify the injunction to appoint an independent monitor to oversee the center’s actions and ensure trustees receive necessary information.





FROM VIRGINIA

A 17-year-old Loudoun County student was charged with a felony and could face between five and 20 years in prison after a fight at Park View High School in Sterling left another student hospitalized with serious injuries, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports.

Fairfax County school employees will soon be able to opt out of staffing weapon-detection systems at school entrances after the school board unanimously approved a teacher’s grievance, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.





SOCIAL CAPITAL

social-capital-option-1-2.jpg (2600x1733, AR: 1.50)
The District has had an eventful month. In the wake of the midterms, nobody knows what this blue wave will feel like, or what will happen to the cultural energy that belonged to MAGA over the past two years. Everything from social circles to the real estate market could be subject to change.

This transitional moment sets the stage for Social Capital, a new weekly column about D.C.’s people, places and parties penned by The Sun’s Sarah Beth Spraggins. You can find the inaugural edition — featuring everyone from Stephen Miller to Mayor Muriel Bowser — right here.





METRO MOMENT


The Bachelor has spoken. Standing in front of a sizable media scrum on Thursday in Ashburn, Commanders quarterback Sam Hartman spoke at length about his decision to star in the ABC dating show.

As expected of a football player participating in reality television, Hartman said he signed on to find his “somebody,” his “second love” (football, of course, being his first) and his “future teammate.” After just a five-minute presser, it’s clear why producers chose Hartman: He’s got what the kids call “rizz.”

“For anyone who’s married, when you went up there and said your vows in front of the ordained, have you ever heard of anyone getting asked where you met?” Hartman mused at one point. “They ask you if you want to do this thing, whether through sickness or through health, and I think that’s the realest it can be.”





SPORTS

Audi Field 1 (3392x2261, AR: 1.50)
How Audi got rowdy: In just a few years, Audi Field has quickly become a comfortable and cacophonous home for the Spirit. The District may have bigger stadiums, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri writes, but it does not have any other that consistently combines “the volume of a rave with the good vibes of a neighborhood block party.” And the players have responded to that passion — Washington has never lost a playoff game at Audi, a streak they hope to continue when they host Saturday’s championship game.

“We are very powerful when we play here,” Spirit coach Adrián González said of Audi and the fans that fill it. “We play connected with them.”

Free Spirit: Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George announced last night that she’ll raffle off 200 pairs of free tickets to Saturday’s game. The tickets, in the fan section, are only for D.C. residents. Enter the raffle here by 11 a.m. today.

What to Watch This Weekend

Friday

NCAAM: Maryland vs. Wagner, 7 p.m. (B1G+)

NBA: Wizards at Bulls, 8 p.m. (Monumental)

Saturday

NCAAW: Maryland vs. Morgan State, noon (BIG+)

NCAAM: Georgetown vs. Coppin State, 6 p.m. (ESPN+)

NCAAF: Maryland at USC, 6:15 p.m. (BTN)

NHL: Capitals at Bruins, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

NWSL Final: Spirit vs. Kansas City Current, 8 p.m. (CBS)

Sunday

NBA: Wizards vs. Magic, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

NFL: Vikings at 49ers, 8:20 p.m. (NBC)






Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: Lame-Duck Trump Gets a Role He Likes: Prized Guest
entries.summary: As Americans begin to look past his presidency, Trump’s Asia trip put the focus on the consequential power he retains on the world stage.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump will step into the White House briefing room Friday to take reporters’ questions after a three-day whirlwind trip to Asia. In stops in the Philippines and China, Trump sought to show that even as Americans seem to be beginning to move on from him, he remains the most consequential figure on the global stage.

“President Trump’s trip to China was the ultimate reminder that while Democrats in Congress may lead a few congressional committees, he continues to lead the free world,” said a MAGA ally close to the White House.

To reinforce that message, Trump postured alongside familiar faces. But instead of appearing with America’s long-standing allies, he cozied up with the leaders of two of the world’s least free countries, according to international watchdogs: China and Russia.

For Trump, a win on the substance wasn’t required. Instead, the White House relied on the symbolism, optics and how he was treated by the host countries. While domestically, Trump has started to feel more disconnected from the larger political picture, the international trip allowed him to play the role he enjoys most: a desired and prized guest.

The trip had all the trappings of a legacy-defining moment, something Trump seeks to burnish in his last two years in office. And people close to the president expect him to flex his influence abroad, even as he faces a contentious relationship with a Democratic-led Congress in the new year.

“He probably figures if he resolves the Ukraine war and Iran dispute then he will save his legacy,” said a Trump administration official who, like others who talked with The Washington Sun, spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals.

In China, the president once again eschewed conventional thinking that American adversaries shouldn’t have a seat at the table. Instead, he walked beside Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin to the most anticipated meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. As Trump flew back to D.C. on Thursday, his White House published a highlight reel on social media of the president meeting with the autocratic leaders.

“It’s usual for presidents to focus abroad in the second half of their term,” Michael Beeman, a former senior Trump U.S. trade official, said in a text message to The Sun after the summit ended.

Bill Clinton and Barack Obama were among those who focused on international issues during the last part of their second terms, including the Israeli-Palestinian peace deal and Iran nuclear negotiations, respectively.

“[It’s] interesting how the attempt to try and re-up the ‘strong man’ vibe came across this time to many as looking weak instead,” Beeman said of Trump’s trip.

The U.S. didn’t play the role of peacemaker this time, unlike during previous high-stakes negotiations. China took the starring role for this event, playing host as well as convening those who came. Many observers said the APEC summit bolstered Xi’s credentials as a statesman on the global stage without making many concessions.

“Xi was really able to demonstrate and create this impression that China now is the kingmaker of all the most powerful countries in the world,” said William Yang, a senior analyst who specializes in Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group. “Jinping proved he is powerful at convening, but also able to dictate and at least shape the agenda to a point where China did not lose much of its core interest.”

Since the summit’s end, Trump has faced harsh criticism for elevating Putin by effectively ending his isolation from the wider international community over his continued war in Ukraine, and it heightened allies’ concern that the U.S. could side with Russia, the aggressor, over Ukraine.

With China arguably at the center of Trump’s trade focus, senior officials have had to engage in several negotiation meetings as the administration seeks to regulate the relationship between the U.S. and its economic rival. It’s a far cry from the past tit-for-tat relationship, in which Trump once accused China of “raping” the American economy with unfair trade practices.

“One of the policy surprises of the second Trump administration, that probably shouldn't have been a surprise, is that the president has elevated a positive bilateral economic relationship with China to be at the top of his foreign policy priorities,” said Andrew Peek, a former deputy assistant secretary of state for Iraq and Iran, who called the trip valuable for the benchmark it created. “I thought it was a useful precedent to set.”

The two countries agreed in May to several deliverables to be finalized after more negotiations, including China’s purchase of 200 Boeing airplanes, an increase in its purchase of U.S. soybeans and the establishment of a board of trade. The negotiations in May — followed by another round when Xi visited Washington in September — also yielded a strategic truce that sought to avoid weaponizing access to critical materials like rare earth minerals.

Administration officials said ahead of Trump’s Asia trip that the central focus of Trump’s meeting with Xi would be the implementation of the trade agreement the U.S. and China entered into in October 2025. China’s slow-walking of the delivery of the rare earth minerals that it agreed to provide to the U.S. has caused frustration within the administration, the officials said. The administration officials also said ahead of the trip that the U.S. would be reluctant to extend the agreement without China promising to make substantive changes.

Though the U.S., Russia and China released a joint statement following Thursday’s meeting, it did not mention whether any of the previous trade issues between the Americans and Chinese had been resolved.

“It seems to be an admission that the ‘old things’ are not going to be worked out but managed — at best — instead,” said Beeman, who led the renegotiations for the U.S.-South Korea free trade agreement and U.S.-Japan trade agreement during Trump’s first term. “That things will just be accepted or tolerated ‘as they are.’”

Instead, the statement noted four points of agreements between the countries: reforms to the United Nations, an increase in oil production, beginning talks on denuclearization and criticism of the International Criminal Court.

The declaration from Trump, Xi and Putin rebuked the ICC, saying the leaders had jointly agreed that the court and similar institutions should not “abuse their jurisdiction.” Specifically, their statement prioritized “state consent and immunities of State officials.”

Proponents of the ICC say its founding document, the Rome Statute, which the U.S. helped craft, rejects immunity for government officials for violating international law. The court has an active warrant for Putin over apparent war crimes against Ukrainian children, and legal experts have suggested the Trump administration’s attacks on alleged drug boats could constitute international crimes. And while the argument of “consent” has been cited to challenge ICC warrants against Israeli officials such as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over actions in Gaza, some have argued that the ICC doesn’t have jurisdiction because Israel has not joined the court. But global affairs experts have noted that the ICC is permitted to probe incidents involving member states, which include Ukraine and the Palestinian state.

Mark Kersten, a professor of human rights law at Canada’s University of the Fraser Valley, told The Sun the remarks from Trump, Xi and Putin this week risk encouraging future rights abuses internationally and an expanding sense of impunity.

“China does not find itself in the crosshairs of an ICC investigation but perhaps … is seeking to try to ensure any atrocities that it may commit in neighboring countries or wherever it may be can never be prosecuted or investigated,” he said. “It is obviously in Putin's direct interest for the United States to destroy or dismantle or neuter the International Criminal Court.”

The Trump administration has slapped unprecedented sanctions on the ICC.

“The fact that we saw Trump now in recent weeks say that he’s doing this to protect Putin and to protect Netanyahu is exactly why member states of the International Criminal Court should say, ‘Absolutely not — we will not negotiate the future of the ICC over the barrel of a gun,’” Kersten said.

Observers also suspect Washington may target the International Court of Justice, the top court of the United Nations, if it rules in favor of the accusation from South Africa and other countries that Israel has committed a genocide in Gaza.

Israel denies the claim and is battling the suit. Also on Thursday, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya people, in a case seen as a key indicator for how the court may rule on Gaza next year.

Trump is scheduled to meet again with Xi and even perhaps Putin next month when he hosts the G20 summit at his resort in Doral, Florida, an event that’s expected to provide similar pomp and pageantry that was on display this week.

The president is expected to continue to tout the relationship-building focus of his foreign policy — something his supporters believe only he can do.

“They both like Trump,” the president told Fox News ahead of the trilateral meeting of his relationship with Xi and Putin. “Now, what happens after me? That I can’t tell you.”

entries.title: ‘Eric’s ID Law’ Butterflies to Be Offered to Montgomery County Students
entries.summary: The small black butterfly symbol would appear on the front of the student’s ID badge to indicate they have a nonapparent disability.
entries.content:
The butterfly symbol that Maryland residents with hidden disabilities can feature on their state-issued IDs will soon be offered to students in Montgomery County Public Schools.

The symbol, introduced in a state law passed last year, aims to alert first responders and others that the ID holder may have communication challenges or specific needs that are not immediately apparent, helping reduce unnecessary stress and misunderstanding during routine interactions.

Superintendent Thomas Taylor said at a board of education meeting on Thursday that Montgomery County schools will begin allowing students, with family consent, to request removable butterfly stickers for their badges in January as part of a pilot program.

He said the county expects to expand the program and begin offering the butterfly symbol on newly issued student ID badges at the start of next school year.

“A small butterfly, a simple symbol, but a powerful message,” Taylor said at the meeting. “Whether it’s in a busy hallway, on a school bus or during an emergency, that butterfly is a reminder to slow down, show patience and lead with understanding.”

Eric Carpenter-Grantham, who was diagnosed with autism at 3 years old, strove to have “Eric’s ID Law” passed following the murder of George Floyd, fearing that law enforcement may misread how people on the spectrum react during interactions. Since the law passed in October 2025, more than 34,000 Marylanders have had the butterfly symbol placed on their driver's license, ID or moped permit.

Similar to organ donor and veteran symbols, the butterfly appears on the front of the card and is free.
Butterfly ID (3500x2625, AR: 1.33)Carpenter-Grantham told The Washington Sun in a statement that he moved to Montgomery County with his mom in 2014 because they believed the county’s schools offered stronger special education programs and resources to better support his educational needs. He graduated from John F. Kennedy High School in 2023.

“I’m proud to be the only member of my family to graduate from Montgomery County Public Schools,” Carpenter-Grantham said during the meeting. “It is an honor seeing Eric’s ID butterfly entering Montgomery County Public Schools, making this the first school system in the nation to bring the butterfly symbol into the public schools for students with nonapparent disabilities.”

He has been pushing for every state in the country to pass the ID law. Lawmakers have introduced similar bills in New York and Delaware. And last week, Mayor Muriel Bowser signed Eric’s ID Amendment Act of 2026 into law, allowing D.C. residents to request the butterfly symbol on their driver’s license, permit or ID without submitting proof of a nonapparent disability.

“But I want everybody to remember something: The job is not finished yet,” Carpenter-Grantham said during Wednesday’s D.C. Board of Education meeting. “Our mission is to continue spreading the word of ‘Eric’s ID Law’ and making sure that people in the District of Columbia with autism, intellectual disabilities and nonapparent disabilities and other disabilities are recognized, respected and understood.”

Carpenter-Grantham said during Thursday’s Montgomery County meeting that the butterfly symbol was also recently implemented at Montgomery College, where he is currently enrolled, and that more than 40 students there have already obtained the butterfly on their school IDs. He added that Montgomery County public libraries will soon offer the butterfly on their cards as well.

“I wish this initiative had existed when I was a student,” Carpenter-Grantham said. “Knowing that today’s students will have this opportunity is a blessing and a dream come true. The butterfly represents hope, peace, freedom and change, and we pray that this symbol will empower students to use their voices and embrace who they are.”
entries.author: Justice Covert

entries.title: Trump Administration Says It Can Detonate Iowa Lead Despite Court Order
entries.summary: In a court filing, a DOJ attorney said the Army has the authority to blow up the lead explosives even if a judge blocks the EPA permit currently allowing the plan.
entries.content:
The Trump administration said the Army has the authority to detonate lead explosives in Iowa as early as Monday, even though a federal court has temporarily blocked its environmental permit to do so.

The Army has briefly delayed its planned detonation of 68 barrels of degrading lead azide after widespread pushback from Iowa and Illinois leaders, and environmental groups sued to delay the planned detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

A federal appeals court placed an administrative stay on the Army’s emergency permit for the detonation while it decides the case, but on Friday a Justice Department attorney told the court an Environmental Protection Agency regulation would allow the Army to move forward anyway.

The Army, which is not a part of the lawsuit, could proceed with the planned explosion without a permit if it determines there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment,” the DOJ filing says.

Army officials are concerned that the degrading and volatile lead explosive will detonate on its own in an uncontrolled manner as the weather gets colder. When the Army announced it would delay the planned explosion from Friday to Monday, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle described the new date as “the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

The forecast for Middletown, Iowa — where the plant is located — shows temperatures dropping significantly on Sunday night and then again on Monday night.

Iowa and Illinois leaders had called for greater communication with communities that could be affected by the explosion. Both the Iowa governor and many communities in Iowa and Illinois said they did not learn about the Army’s plans to detonate the lead until just five days before the scheduled explosion date, when the Army published maps that showed the possibility of a plume of lead dust stretching far beyond the ammunition plant.

Thien Chau, an Earthjustice attorney representing the plaintiffs, said the DOJ points to a specific regulation in its filing that is “an extraordinary and extreme backstop for situations where there is truly nothing else that can be done.”

“It is an incredibly high bar, and we strongly urge the Army not to rely on it if it is only to sidestep the ongoing processes to obtain transparency and protections that communities, government leaders, and the law are all currently demanding,” Chau said.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has not yet provided any further information about when the court might ask for a hearing or issue a decision on the plaintiffs’ emergency motion for a stay. The decision to temporarily block the EPA’s permit for the explosion was one sentence.

The DOJ said in its filing Friday that it will file a response to that emergency motion before Monday.

On Friday, after the judge temporarily blocked the EPA permit, the Army issued a public statement alongside the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services that did not acknowledge the judge’s decision.

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise,” the agencies said in a joint statement.
